rows.description: A toddler who is hungry cannot say so and shows it through crying, grabbing, throwing food or refusing everything. Feeding on a regular rhythm often ends the tantrum faster than any discipline.

rows.subtype: Teen growth spurt appetite and grumpiness [Actor]
rows.description: A growing teenager gets sharp and low when meals are late because the body is demanding fuel. Recognising the pattern lets the teen say I need to eat before we talk instead of blaming everyone around.
A busy professional skips lunch to finish a task, then writes a harsh email or feels hopeless about work. Low fuel narrows patience and makes problems look larger than they are.
A child loves showing a younger sibling how to tie shoes or draw, feeling proud to be the one who knows. This early urge to pass something on is the seed of later generativity.
A young adult volunteers, mentors school kids or builds a small project not for credit but because they want their effort to outlast them. It sits alongside ambition, not in place of it.
A young worker settles into a routine, thinks only of salary and comfort, and feels flat when asked what they are building. It is not laziness; it is a life turned entirely inward.

A parent facing a shouting child may respond louder, which escalates the storm. Lowering the voice, pausing and returning to the conversation once both are calm models the skill being asked of the child.

rows.subtype: Hostel argument that got out of hand [Receiver]
rows.description: A young adult on the receiving end of shouted words feels shock, fear or a rising wish to hit back. Keeping distance and refusing to match the volume protects safety and often lets the other person deflate.

rows.subtype: Feeling scared means it is dangerous [Actor]
rows.description: A child who feels nervous about a new swimming class insists the pool is dangerous; the strength of the feeling is taken as proof about the world.

rows.subtype: I feel useless so I am [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager feels heavy and ashamed after a failed test and decides they must be worthless; the mood is treated as a fact about who they are.

rows.subtype: Feeling guilty so must be guilty [Actor]
rows.description: A student feels guilty about a friend's low mood and assumes they caused it; guilt is a feeling and is not evidence of wrongdoing, though it can point to what one values.
A young adult sits with an elder and lets the same story be told again, asking a new question each time. Elders often want to be heard and remembered more than to instruct.
A young adult explains a phone feature or a doctor's advice slowly, without teasing, and lets the elder do the steps. Preserving an elder's dignity matters as much as the task.

A teenager says huh as confusion, surprise or challenge and mm-hmm as listening, agreement or a brush-off. Tone and timing shape meaning, so a follow-up question is wiser than assuming the sound means yes.

rows.subtype: Wow, ooh and ah in messages [Mismatch]
rows.description: A young adult reads wow in a text as admiration, shock or sarcasm depending on tone and emoji. Without a voice the reader can misjudge, so clear words or a follow-up call keep sarcasm from causing hurt.
